activities.anchor: not one, anywhere, in the history of the cosmos
activities.caption: call the magnitude — Sirius's furious burn rate
activities.name: slSiriusEstimate

config.prompt: The M^3.5 rule: Sirius A is about 2 solar masses. Roughly what multiple of the Sun's luminosity does that give it?
config.why: 2^3.5 ≈ 11× the Sun's light — and its lifetime falls to 10,000/2^2.5 ≈ 1,800 million years, six times shorter. Big stars die young.
config.context: A red dwarf at 0.2 M would live 5,600,000 million years — 400× the age of the universe. No red dwarf has ever died.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — from cloud to main sequence
activities.name: slBirthCloze

config.text: A star begins as a %%0%% that collapses and fragments into knots; each knot heats until its core reaches about %%1%% million kelvin, where hydrogen fuses into %%2%% — and the star settles onto the main sequence.
config.hint: The nursery is visible in Orion, 1,300 light years away.

activities.caption: true or false — how stars actually shine
activities.name: slFusionJudge

statements.s: Stars burn fuel the way a fire burns wood.
statements.why: No flame is involved — fusion is nuclei merging under enormous temperature and pressure.

statements.s: Fusion releases energy because the products weigh slightly less than the inputs.
statements.why: The missing mass is the energy — which is why the tank is measured in billions of years.

statements.s: Chemical burning is trillions of times less efficient than fusion.
statements.why: Which is exactly why the fuel tank runs in billions of years.

statements.s: A protostar glows in infrared while still gathering mass from its disc.
statements.why: Gravitational energy converting to kinetic — visible in the Orion Nebula's nurseries.

activities.anchor: the standard candles — below — take over
activities.caption: place Sirius on the magnitude scale
activities.name: slSiriusPlace

config.prompt: Apparent magnitude runs backwards — brighter is smaller. Place Sirius on the scale:
config.why: Sirius: −1.5; the naked-eye limit is +6; the Sun blazes at −26.7. Five steps of magnitude = a factor of 100 in brightness.
config.context: The base of the distance ladder: one arcsecond of parallax defines the parsec, 3.26 light years.

activities.anchor: defined absolute magnitude at a standard distance
activities.caption: bet first — two stars, equal brightness
activities.name: slBrightPredict

config.q: Two stars look exactly equally bright in the sky. What do you actually know about them?
choices: Nothing separable yet — brightness mixes luminosity and distance, and you must break the mix apart
config.why: Brightness as seen mixes two unknowns — which is why astronomers defined absolute magnitude at a standard 10 parsecs.

activities.anchor: the plot of stellar evolution itself
activities.caption: pair each H–R region with its residents
activities.name: slHRMatch

config.prompt: The most organising picture in astronomy — match region to resident:

pairs.right: hydrogen-burning adulthood; position fixed by mass
blue, over 30,000 K, rare — and doomed

config.why: The main sequence is a weighing scale, not a path: where a star sits is fixed by mass, and it leaves only when the fuel runs out.

activities.anchor: not yet old enough to contain a single example of
activities.caption: file the endings — which road does each fact belong to?
activities.name: slEndingsBuckets

config.prompt: Two endings, one boundary at 1.4 solar masses. File each fact:

items.label: the Sun swells past Mercury and Venus
the envelope blown off gently as a planetary nebula
the core passes 1.4 solar masses and degeneracy pressure fails
Chandrasekhar derived the boundary, aged 19, on a ship to England

config.why: Derived in 1930, Nobel in 1983 — the limit is why the gentle road ends where it does.

activities.anchor: band needs its own kind of eye
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the first rule of telescopes
activities.name: tlApertureCloze

config.text: Light-gathering grows with the %%0%% of the objective, so doubling the diameter quadruples the photons. The 10-metre Keck telescopes collect on the order of a %%1%% times more light than your dark-adapted eye.
config.hint: Aperture beats everything — and the leaps accelerate as you go bigger.

activities.caption: pair each design piece with its consequence
activities.name: tlDesignMatch

config.prompt: Lens versus mirror, eyepiece versus aperture:

pairs.right: chromatic aberration, and rim-only support that sags at scale
all wavelengths focus identically, supported from behind
decided at purchase, unchangeable — the number that matters

config.why: Every large modern telescope — Keck 10 m, Rubin 8.4 m, the 39-metre ELT — is a reflector, for mechanical reasons: the look is 1609's, not the physics'.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the 250× trap
activities.name: tlMagnifySpot

config.prompt: One line of this eyepiece answer is wrong — click it:
lines: A 1,000 mm reflector with a 25 mm eyepiece magnifies 1,000 ÷ 25 = 40×.
Swap to a 10 mm eyepiece: 100× — more detail through the same tube.
Swap to a 4 mm eyepiece: 250× — now the maximum useful detail, since magnification always adds resolution.
The practical hierarchy: aperture first, magnification second — only as much as the aperture supports.
config.correction: 250× through a 10 cm aperture exceeds the useful limit (~2× aperture in mm = 200×) — the image grows dimmer and mushier, not more detailed.
config.why: Magnification without aperture is empty magnification: enlarging a blur gives a bigger blur.

config.prompt: A 10 cm telescope resolves about 1.4 arcseconds; Hubble's 2.4 m mirror resolves about 0.06. Roughly how many times finer is Hubble's resolution?
config.why: 1.4 ÷ 0.06 ≈ 23× finer — enough to separate individual stars in neighbouring galaxies.
config.context: θ ≈ 1.22λ/D: bigger D means sharper images — the second dividend of aperture, after light-gathering.

activities.anchor: the least informative number on the box
activities.caption: bet first — the box's 600× claim
activities.name: tlBoxPredict

config.q: A shop telescope advertises '600× magnification!' on a 60 mm lens. What does that number actually tell you?
choices: Nothing useful — 600× exceeds the useful limit (~2× aperture in mm) and enlarges a blur
You will see 600× more detail than the naked eye
The telescope gathers 600× more light than the eye
config.why: Empty magnification: the diffraction limit caps the detail no matter how far you stretch it. Aperture buys light and resolution; magnification is eyepiece arithmetic.

activities.anchor: the detector came first, and the universe followed
activities.caption: file the bands — ground window or orbital mission?
activities.name: tlBandBuckets

config.prompt: The atmosphere is a filter with two clean windows. File each band:

items.label: radio — pulsars, quasars, the cosmic microwave background
optical — with adaptive optics and laser guide stars
infrared — water vapour swallows it; Webb must even cool its own mirror to −230 °C
X-ray and gamma — photons stop in matter outright

config.why: The filter is protective for life and obstructive for astronomy — each orbiting telescope is a mission to a wavelength the ground can never see.

activities.anchor: What the eye cannot see, it cannot even suspect
activities.caption: true or false — Galileo's eighteen months
activities.name: tlGalileoJudge

statements.s: Venus's full phases proved it circles the Sun — under Ptolemy it could only ever show crescents.
statements.why: One modest-looking observation through a poor lens, and half the cosmology falls.

statements.s: Galileo estimated lunar mountain heights from the terminator's shadows — some taller than any then known on Earth.
statements.why: The Moon's edge was rough, not the perfect sphere philosophy demanded.

statements.s: Jupiter's four moons proved that everything orbits the Earth.
statements.why: They proved the opposite: not everything orbited the Earth.

statements.s: A new instrument is a better view of the same universe.
statements.why: It is a different universe — radio found pulsars (Bell, 1967), X-rays found accreting black holes, infrared found the nurseries behind dust.

activities.anchor: photons the eye could never catch
activities.caption: rebuild the counting experiment
activities.name: photonCountOrder

config.prompt: An image is not a window but a count — put the sequence in order:
items: The objective intercepts photons over minutes or hours of exposure
Faintness, detail and colour are set by how many photons were caught and how faithfully counted
Telescope time is scheduled in committee-reviewed blocks — exposure is a real cost
config.why: Professional observing is closer to running a counting experiment than to looking: the difference between 4 m and 8 m is not what you can see but what you can measure in the same night.
